sentences.show: In 1969, a killer mailed a secret code to a San Francisco newspaper. It took 51 years to crack it.
He called himself the Zodiac. In less than a year, he attacked seven people around San Francisco Bay. Five of them died.
Young couples, on lonely country roads. Then a taxi driver, in the middle of the city.
Then came the letters. Signed with a crosshair, and a demand: print this on the front page.
Inside were ciphers. The first one was cracked within days, by an ordinary couple in Salinas.
It said he liked killing, and that his victims would be his slaves in the afterlife.
But the next one, 340 symbols, beat everyone who tried, for half a century.
Then, in December 2020, three amateurs in America, Australia and Belgium ran 650,000 possible keys through a computer.
And it cracked. The FBI confirmed it.
The first line: "I hope you are having lots of fun in trying to catch me."
He wasn't afraid of the gas chamber, he wrote, because it would send him to paradise all the sooner.
But no name. Police only ever named one suspect, Arthur Leigh Allen. He died in 1992, never charged.
Two of his ciphers are still unsolved. One of them begins: "My name is…"
So the Zodiac may have told us exactly who he was. We just can't read it.
His last code is still unsolved. This one's easy: subscribe.
